Circuit Analysis: Energy, Dividers, Kirchhoff's Laws, Bridges, and Op-Amp Gain

Unit 2: Fundamentals of Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 13 of 60 in CBET Academy.

The exam's electronics items are short calculations. Each one below is a formula, a worked example, and the mistake the distractors are built from.

Energy and the kilowatt-hour

Power is the rate of energy use; energy is power times time. A device drawing 500 mA at 120 V uses 0.5 x 120 = 60 W; run for 8 hours it uses 60 x 8 = 480 watt-hours = 0.48 kWh, the unit on the electric bill. P = V x I, P = I squared x R, P = V squared / R: a 10 A current through 30 ohms dissipates 100 x 30 = 3,000 W.

Equivalent resistance

Series adds: 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 ohms. Parallel uses reciprocals: for 4, 8, and 5 ohms, 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/5 = 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.2 = 0.575, so R = 1 / 0.575 = 1.74 ohms, smaller than the smallest branch. For two resistors the shortcut is product over sum.

Voltage divider

In series, each resistor takes a share of the source voltage in proportion to its resistance: V across R1 = V source x R1 / (R1 + R2 + ...). A 10 V source across 1.5 kilohms and 1 kilohm in series puts 10 x 1000 / 2500 = 4 V across the 1 kilohm resistor. Every resistor in a series string obeys the same rule; the shares add back to the source.

Current divider

In parallel, the current splits in inverse proportion to resistance: I through a branch = I total x (1 / R branch) / (sum of 1 / R for all branches). With 600 mA feeding 80, 50, and 200 ohm branches, the 50 ohm branch gets 600 x (1/50) / (1/80 + 1/50 + 1/200) = 600 x 0.02 / 0.0375 = 320 mA. The smallest resistance takes the biggest share. A quicker check: all parallel branches see the same voltage, so I = V / R for each.

Kirchhoff's laws, used properly

  • KCL (current law): current into a node equals current out. Nodal analysis: if 9 A enters and 5 A and 2 A leave on two branches, the third branch carries 2 A. A negative answer means the current flows opposite the arrow you assumed.
  • KVL (voltage law): the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero; rises equal drops. Mesh analysis: a 10 V source and drops of 3, 2, and 4 V leave 1 V for the last element.

These let you solve any unknown from a schematic when the resistor formulas alone will not.

A battery's internal resistance

A real battery is an ideal source in series with a small resistance. If an open-circuit 1.58 V cell drops to 1.46 V with an 80 ohm load, the load current is 1.46 / 80 = 0.01825 A, and the internal resistance is the lost voltage over that current: (1.58 minus 1.46) / 0.01825 = 6.58 ohms. Internal resistance rises as a battery ages, which is why an old battery reads full voltage unloaded and collapses under load.

The Wheatstone bridge

Four resistors in a diamond with a meter across the middle. The bridge is balanced (zero current in the meter) when the ratios of the two sides match: R1 / R2 = R3 / R4. Given three values, the unknown is R4 = R3 x R2 / R1: with 9.8, 5.8, and 1.9 ohms, the missing resistance is 9.8 / 5.8 x 1.9 = 3.2 ohms. Strain gauge pressure transducers and thermistor circuits are bridges; the tiny imbalance is the signal.

Op-amp gain from resistor ratios

For an inverting amplifier, gain = R feedback / R input (the sign inverts). A gain of 9 with a 5 kilohm input resistor needs a 45 kilohm feedback resistor. Non-inverting gain is 1 + R feedback / R input. ECG and pressure amplifiers are built from these ratios; a drifted resistor is a wrong gain.

Exam tip: energy is power times time, in kWh on the bill. Divider formulas: voltage splits in proportion to resistance in series; current splits inversely in parallel. KCL at nodes, KVL around loops. Internal resistance is the voltage drop under load divided by the load current. A bridge balances when the ratios match. Inverting op-amp gain is R feedback over R input.
Remember
P = VI = I squared R = V squared / R; energy = P x t, kWh. Series adds; parallel reciprocals, less than the smallest. Voltage divider: V x R1 / R total. Current divider: inverse to resistance. KCL in equals out; KVL loop sums to zero. Internal resistance = voltage drop / load current. Wheatstone balanced when R1/R2 = R3/R4. Inverting gain = Rf / Rin.
Deeper explanation

Circuit Analysis: Energy, Dividers, Kirchhoff's Laws, Bridges, and Op-Amp Gain, explained slowly

Calculation questions are pattern questions

Every electronics calculation on the exam is one of a handful of patterns. Recognize the pattern, write the formula, substitute, and check the answer against a sanity rule (parallel resistance is smaller than any branch; divider shares add to the source; currents into a node equal currents out). The wrong options are always the result of using the wrong pattern.

Pattern 1: energy from power and time

given                        formula                    example
V and I                      P = V x I                  120 V x 0.5 A = 60 W
I and R                      P = I squared x R          10 A, 30 ohms: 100 x 30 = 3,000 W = 3 kW
V and R                      P = V squared / R          120 V, 60 ohms: 14,400 / 60 = 240 W
P and time                   E = P x t                  60 W x 8 h = 480 Wh = 0.48 kWh

Sanity check: kilowatt-hours are energy; kilowatts are power. Bills are in kWh.

Pattern 2: equivalent resistance

Series: add. Parallel: add reciprocals and invert, or product over sum for two.

4, 8, 5 ohms in parallel:  1/4 + 1/8 + 1/5 = 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.2 = 0.575;  R = 1 / 0.575 = 1.74 ohms
120-ohm resistor in series with two 60-ohm resistors in parallel:  60 || 60 = 30;  30 + 120 = 150 ohms

Drawing check: two components in parallel share both end nodes; in series they share exactly one node with nothing else attached.

Pattern 3: dividers

voltage divider (series)     V across Rx = V source x Rx / R total
   10 V across 1.5 k and 1 k:  V across 1 k = 10 x 1000 / 2500 = 4 V
   120 V across 60 and 100:    V across 60 = 120 x 60 / 160 = 45 V
   12 V across 10, 20, and (15 || 30 = 10): total 40; V across the parallel pair = 12 x 10 / 40 = 3 V, the same across the 30 as across the 15
current divider (parallel)   I through Rx = I total x (1/Rx) / (sum of 1/R)
   600 mA into 80, 50, 200:   1/80 + 1/50 + 1/200 = 0.0125 + 0.02 + 0.005 = 0.0375; I(50) = 600 x 0.02 / 0.0375 = 320 mA
   240 V across a 60-ohm branch: I = 240 / 60 = 4 A regardless of the other branches

Sanity: the biggest resistor takes the biggest voltage in series and the smallest current in parallel.

Pattern 4: Kirchhoff

KCL at a node:   9 A in = 5 A + 2 A + I1 out  ->  I1 = 2 A
KCL with a sign: 3 + I2 + 6 = 2 + 3 + 1  ->  I2 = -3 A (3 A the other way)
KVL in a loop:   -10 + 3 + 2 + 4 + V = 0  ->  V = 1 V

Nodal analysis uses KCL at nodes; mesh analysis uses KVL around loops. A negative result only means your assumed direction was backward.

Pattern 5: internal resistance

open-circuit voltage 1.58 V; loaded voltage 1.46 V with 80 ohms
I = 1.46 / 80 = 0.01825 A
r internal = (1.58 - 1.46) / 0.01825 = 6.58 ohms

The lost voltage is dropped inside the battery. A tired battery has high internal resistance: full voltage on the meter, nothing under load.

Pattern 6: the bridge

balanced when R1 / R2 = R3 / R4  (no current through the center meter)
R1 = 9.8, R2 = 5.8, R3 = 1.9:  R4 = R3 x R2 / R1 = 1.9 x 5.8 / 9.8 = 1.12?  careful with which resistor is which:
   the guide's arrangement gives Rx = (R1 / R2) x R3 = (9.8 / 5.8) x 1.9 = 3.2 ohms

The lesson: write the ratio from the diagram, solve for the unknown, and check that the two side ratios match. Strain gauges and thermistors sit in bridges so a tiny resistance change becomes a measurable voltage.

Pattern 7: op-amp gain

Inverting: gain = R feedback / R input (output inverted). Gain 9 with R in = 5 kilohms means R f = 45 kilohms. Non-inverting: 1 + R f / R in. A drifted feedback resistor changes the gain, which shows up as a wrong calibration.

How the exam asks it

  • "A bulb draws 500 mA at 120 V for 8 hours; energy used?" 0.48 kWh.
  • "Power with 10 A through 30 ohms?" 3 kW.
  • "Voltage across the 60-ohm resistor in series with 100 ohms on 120 V?" 45 V.
  • "Current through the 50-ohm branch of 80, 50, 200 with 600 mA?" 320 mA.
  • "I1 when 9 A enters and 5 A and 2 A leave?" 2 A.
  • "Internal resistance from 1.58 V dropping to 1.46 V into 80 ohms?" 6.58 ohms.
  • "R2 for gain 9 with R1 = 5 k?" 45 k.

What to memorize

  • P = VI = I squared R = V squared / R; E = P x t; kWh.
  • Series adds; parallel reciprocals; two in parallel: product over sum.
  • Voltage divider proportional to R; current divider inversely proportional to R.
  • KCL: in equals out; KVL: loop sums to zero.
  • Internal resistance = voltage drop / load current.
  • Bridge balance: equal ratios. Inverting gain = Rf / Rin.
